query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning-driven, high-throughput composition-screening approach can identify new refractory high-entropy alloys with higher strength, improved ductility, and lower density than RHEAs designed solely by conventional thermodynamic or trial-and-error methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A polycrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy near equiatomic composition (e.g., Nb-Ti-V-Zr) produced via standard melting and casting routes.
generation.intervention: Employ an integrated high-throughput computational strategy that uses machine-learning models to predict mechanical properties and density from elemental compositions, iterating on any newly tested data to refine model accuracy and identify optimal compositions.
generation.conditions: Exploration of multi-principal RHEA composition space; mechanical testing at room and elevated temperatures; systematic tracking of density, yield strength, and tensile ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: Body-centered cubic matrix with possible precipitation strengthening phases determined by multivariate composition predictions.
generation.mechanism: Machine learning captures the complex synergistic effects of multiple principal elements, guiding compositions toward enhanced solid-solution and precipitation strengthening while maintaining low density.
generation.predicted_outcome: ML-optimized alloys will achieve a measurable increase in yield strength (above conventional RHEA baselines) and ductility, accompanied by a decreased average density, relative to compositions designed through purely manual or thermodynamic approaches.
generation.baseline: Existing refractory HEA compositions derived from conventional CALPHAD or heuristic-based methods for similar target properties.
generation.boundary: Accuracy and generality of the ML-based predictions may degrade if the training dataset does not adequately represent higher-order chemical interactions or off-equiatomic compositions.
generation.uncertainty: While proof-of-concept results exist, refinements to the machine-learning models and expansion of the training data are needed before broad generalization on all RHEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Systematically synthesize candidate compositions predicted by the machine-learning model alongside control alloys from prior design methods to measure mechanical properties and density.
measurements: Room- and high-temperature tensile tests to determine yield strength and elongation.
Microstructure characterization (SEM, XRD) to identify phases.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-optimized alloys fail to exceed both the yield strength and ductility of the control alloys while maintaining a lower relative density, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
